lead: A neck bridge, or wrestler's bridge, is a bodyweight position in which a person arches the body with weight carried on the feet and the head or neck. It comes from wrestling and grappling, where bridging is used to escape pins, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to thicken the neck. The appearance idea is that loading the neck muscles with bodyweight builds a bigger, stronger-looking neck that frames the jaw and balances the shoulders and upper body.

The general bridge exercise is described on Wikipedia as intended to improve lower-back and gluteal strength, and bridging appears in the list of techniques used in judo, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, mixed martial arts, wrestling and other martial arts.[1] The article covers hands-and-feet variations such as the bridge hold, bridge push-up and wall walking, and does not describe the head-supported wrestler's bridge or any safety guidance.[1]
No study has tested neck bridges for cosmetic neck thickness.

angle.text: People who use neck bridges say that carrying bodyweight on the head and neck strengthens and enlarges the neck muscles, which gives a thicker neck that makes the frame look more powerful. The idea carries over from the use of bridging in wrestling.

infobox: Neck, upper back, spinal erectors, glutes, hamstrings

paras: Bridge exercises arch the body so that only some points touch the ground. The common gymnastic bridge rests on hands and feet; the wrestler's bridge rests on the feet and the head or neck. Variations in the general bridge family include static holds, bridge push-ups, one-arm and one-leg versions, wall walking and closing from standing, which load the hamstrings, glutes and spinal erectors.[1]
In wrestling and other grappling sports bridging is used to escape pins, which is why the neck-supported version is associated with those sports.[1]

The sternocleidomastoid is one of the largest and most superficial neck muscles, running from the sternum and collarbone to the skull behind the ear. It rotates and flexes the head and is easy to see and feel on each side of the neck.[2] Deeper and posterior neck muscles, along with the trapezius, which shares its nerve supply, also contribute to neck width and to the line from head to shoulders.[2] These are the muscles that neck-training advocates aim to enlarge.

Neck bridges are mentioned alongside other neck exercises as an inexpensive way to train the neck without equipment. Looksmaxxing discussions about neck size generally pair training with eating enough to gain muscle.
The general bridge article does not discuss the risks of neck-loaded bridging.[1] No injury-rate data for cosmetic neck bridging have been published.
No studies found. Medical literature on 'neck-bridge' devices concerns aneurysm treatment and is unrelated to the exercise.

name: Neck bridges / wrestler bridges

card.summary: A wrestling-style arch on the head and feet used to thicken the neck; no appearance research exists.
card.note: No data on injury risk for this use; the source material is thin.

quick.overview:
A neck bridge is an arch where the head or neck helps support the body, drawn from wrestling and grappling sports.

It is mentioned as a way to thicken the neck. No studies have tested it for that purpose.
quick.mechanism: The position loads the neck and back muscles with bodyweight. General bridge references focus on back and glute strength.
quick.risks: No injury data for cosmetic neck bridging were found. Any risks are not documented in the available sources.
